newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S HANEKOM WINS FIRST ROUND AGAINST KWV.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S HANEKOM WINS FIRST ROUND AGAINST KWV.

text.p: A South African court on Tuesday ruled in favour of Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom's bid to delay the conversion of wine and spirits co-operative KWV into a private company.

KWV, statutory regulator of the wine industry, had planned to complete the conversion by the end of April but the Cape Town court granted an application by Hanekom that effectively suspended the process at least until August 18, when both sides will return to court.

Hanekom sought the postponement to allow further study of his concerns that the KWV plan would lead to state assets being transferred to private hands, to KWV gaining an unfair market advantage and to a regulatory vacuum being created in the industry.
The minister welcomed the court decision but KWV Chairman Lourens Jonker said the co-operative, which markets wine and brandy in about 50 countries, was "extremely disappointed".
"This conversion is now supported by wholesalers -- through the Cape Wine and Spirit Institute -- as being a step which is in the interest of the whole South African wine industry," he said.
"We believe this delay will lead to further abortive expenses for both KWV and the taxpayer," Jonker said.

"No postponement will distract KWV from its objective to convert to a company in the interest of the consumers in its international markets and of the broad South African wine community and its workers."
Jonker said every day lost was costing KWV business opportunities and was also delaying one of the aims Hanekom hopes to achieve, the entry of blacks into the industry.
Hanekom said in a statement that he had no wish to hamper KWV's efforts to become more competitive and develop foreign markets.
But he added that he hoped the court-ordered delay would allow all the parties to arrive at a negotiated settlement "that addresses all the major issues".

"I would like to see a new dispensation for the wine industry where the interests of everyone including new entrants -- growers, producers, workers, wholesalers and consumers -- are addressed," he said.
